title: Playing with a controller without losing the prompts
target: How to move Supermarket Simulator onto a controller without fighting the interface: what the game redraws for you, why a screen can still show key pictures, how a menu is walked, where typing goes, and where vibration actually comes from.
version: 1.6.0 (223), read from the copy of the game this site was built from (see the sources page)
prerequisites: A shop that is open and running
A controller connected and recognised by the machine
A screen you can watch the prompts change on

steps.do: Switch to the pad and let the game redraw the prompts rather than rebinding anything first.
steps.because: the game carries a switch and a deeper switch for the pad along with an icon switcher, so what is shown for an action is chosen rather than bound by hand (GamepadSwitch, GamepadDeepSwitch, GamepadIconSwitcher)

steps.do: If one screen still shows key pictures, look at that screen's layout before you touch your bindings.
steps.because: there is a dispatcher for the pad layout, so a screen can be toggled for a pad separately from the global switch (GamepadLayoutToggleDispatcher)

steps.do: Expect to walk through a menu instead of pointing at it.
steps.because: menu items are made selectable for a pad and the focus is checked, which is why a selection moves down a list rather than a pointer sweeping across it (GamepadUISelectable, CheckGamepadFocus)

steps.do: When something will not become selectable, look for a missing selectable parent rather than rebinding the button.
steps.because: selectable parents are what make a list behave under a pad, and there is even a separate one for a bill entry (GamepadSelectableParent, GamepadSelectableParentBill)

steps.do: Keep the controller in your hands when a name or a search needs text.
steps.because: text entry is handed to a virtual keyboard while a pad is in use rather than forcing you back to the keyboard (VirtualKeyboardGamepadSwitchListener)

steps.do: Judge vibration by the game's own haptic settings, not by the pad's.
steps.because: there is a haptic manager with patterns, durations and a preset configuration behind it, so what the pad does is chosen by the game (HapticManager, HapticPattern, HapticDuration, HapticPresetConfig)

steps.do: Do not assume one screen's behaviour carries to the next.
steps.because: whole screens have handlers of their own, including the vending machine, its computer slot and its individual slots (VendingGamepadHandler, VendingMachineComputerSlot, VendingSlotGamepadParent)

steps.do: Expect the buying screens to rearrange themselves for the pad.
steps.because: the sale items for furniture, paint, produce and loans each carry a pad adjuster of their own (FurnitureSaleItemGamepadUIAdjuster, PaintSaleItemGamepadUIAdjuster, ProducSaleItemGamepadUIAdjuster, LoanItemGamepadUIAdjuster)

steps.do: Treat a missing button picture as a prompt problem rather than a lost input.
steps.because: the game ships its own button pictures for the prompts it draws (XboxOne_A, XboxOne_B, XboxOne_X, XboxOne_Y, KeyboardControllersSpriteAtlas_Cropped_xBox)

commonMistakes: Rebinding buttons when the screen only needed its pad layout toggled.
Expecting a pointer-style menu when the pad walks through selections.
Calling a list broken when it simply has no selectable parent.
Judging vibration by the pad's own software instead of the game's haptic settings.
sources: A local copy of the game, read only. Grounding for each step is on the technical reference pages; no number is estimated.
